newsitem.title: UK: Guinness record book founder leaves for millennium.
newsitem.headline: Guinness record book founder leaves for millennium.

text.p: Norris McWhirter, who started the Guinness Book of Records with twin brother Ross 42 years ago, resigned on Thursday from the book's publishing group to welcome the dawning of the new millennium on a south Pacific island.
McWhirter was editor of the book of superlatives from 1954 to 1986 and has been an editorial adviser for the past 10 years.
Ross was murdered by the Irish Republican Army in 1974 after offering a large reward for information leading to the arrest of IRA bombers seeking to oust Britain from Northern Ireland.
Norris said he had become increasingly divorced from the book's compilation and felt it an appropriate time to leave on the eve of publication of the 1997 edition.
"It's an arduous business promoting the book all over the world," he told Reuters. "I've decided it's time to do what I want to do rather than the thing that I had to do."
Norris will divide his time between books on the 1,043 islands in Britain and the world's inventors, and his plans to create a monopoly on the sighting of the new millenium.
He is chairman of The Millennium Adventure Company which seeks to control territorial and other rights for the filming of the sunrise on January 1, 2000, in the south Pacific.

Pitt Island, one of New Zealand's Chatham Islands, will be "the first terrestrial, accessible and populated place to usher in the next 1,000 years," the statement said. Pitt Island lies around 250 kms (155 miles) west of the international date line.

McWhirter said he had signed up a farmer, Ken Launauze, who had Pitt Island's highest hill on his land. From there, television cameras would catch the first sighting of dawn on the eastern horizon at 3:56 local.
"Perhaps we could get Dame Kiri te Kanawa to sing Morning Has Broken or something," he joked.
"Only the purists will bother about 2001 being the real start of the millennium. They're right of course but just try telling the world's media to sit on their hands for 12 months."
The Guinness Book of Records has sold more than 80 million copies in 350 editions and 37 languages. It is the world's biggest-selling copyright book.
The book was born when Sir Hugh Beaver, managing director of the famous brewery, got into a dispute about whether the golden plover ranked as Europe's fastest game bird.
Beaver, arguing that records invariably started pub and bar disputes the world over, decided it was time to produce the ultimate reference book for superlatives.

Oxford-educated twins Norris and Ross, who were running a fact-finding agency for English newspapers, proved to be the perfect choice as editors. Early editions relied on memories and correspondence as much as printed records.
The book has a built-in obsolescence factor which puts it back in the bestseller lists every year.

Norris reacted to his brother's death, which he likened to an amputation, by forming the Freedom Association. The group aimed to speak for the "silent majority" and fought a number of high-profile battles against officialdom and trade unions.
